question: A 60-year-old woman with bloody urethral discharge has a mobile 1.5 cm lesion at the urethral meatus. Biopsy demonstrates a grade 3 squamous cell carcinoma. Cystoscopy and physical examination are otherwise normal, and staging evaluation is negative. The next step is:

options.E: radical cystectomy and inquinal lymph node dissection.

rationale: Squamous cell cancers of the distal urethra in women may be treated with surgical excision. Location at the urethral meatus, together with the mobile nature of the lesion on examination here, render the tumor likely to be completely excised with distal urethrectomy while preserving the patient's continence. Mapping bladder biopsies would not be necessary to obtain, given the normal cystoscopy and squamous cell histology. Further, while dynamic sentinel lymph node biopsy represents an option for patients with non-palpable inguinal lymph nodes in the setting of a high-risk penile cancer, this approach is not utilized for urethral cancer. Indeed, as no evidence has been found for improved survival after inguinal or pelvic lymphadenectomy among patients with urethral cancer, prophylactic/diagnostic lymph node dissection is not recommended. Chemoradiation has likewise been used in this setting, and multimodal therapy, including chemotherapy, is often recommended for advanced urethral tumors, particularly of the proximal urethra. However, in settings such as in this patient, who has a squamous cell carcinoma without evidence of locally advanced disease, initial chemotherapy alone (i.e., neoadjuvant) has not been demonstrated to improve survival. Radical cystectomy would not be recommended, given the distal location of this tumor.

question: A 58-year-old woman has ypT3bNO urothelial carcinoma of the bladder following neoadjuvant M-VAC and radical cystectomy. Metastatic evaluation is negative and her GFR is normal. The next step is:

options.A: surveillance CT scan in three months.
options.D: two cycles of gemcitabine and cisplatin.

rationale: The correct answer is adjuvant nivolumab, which has been shown to improve disease- free survival in patients with adverse pathology at the time of cystectomy relative to surveillance (pT3, pTa or pN+ in chemotherapy-naive patients or ypT2-4, ypN+ in those who had neoadjuvant chemotherapy). Improvement in disease-free survival was demonstrated in patients with tumors expressing PD-L1 level of 1% or more (HR 0.55) and in the intent-to-treat analysis regardless of PD-L1 expression (HR 0.70), both statistically significant. Atezolizumab has been studied in the adjuvant setting but did not demonstrate a difference in disease-free survival compared with patients who were observed in the IMvigor 010 trial. AUA and NCCN guidelines recommend offering adjuvant chemotherapy to patients with adverse pathology who did not get neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy. However, in this patient who received neoadjuvant M-VAC, gemcitabine and cisplatin would not be indicated. Combination pembrolizumab and enfortumab vedotin has demonstrated superior overall survival compared with chemotherapy in advanced bladder cancer but currently is not indicated in the adjuvant setting.

question: A 63-year-old woman has a 2 cm high-grade Ta bladder cancer. BCG is unavailable locally due to shortage. After TURBT, the next step is:
rationale: This patient has intermediate-risk disease according to the AUA/SUO Guideline classification system. In intermediate-risk patients, there is a substantial risk of disease recurrence and a small risk of disease progression. Accordingly, clinicians should consider a six-week course of intravesical induction immunotherapy (most commonly BCG), after which the clinician should consider maintenance BCG for up to 12 months in those with a complete response. Alternatively, a clinician may use induction intravesical chemotherapy, after which the clinician may utilize maintenance therapy in those with a complete response. Induction BCG and induction chemotherapy have similar efficacy according to available studies and may, therefore, be considered interchangeable. In fact, given the greater risk of adverse events with BCG as compared to most intravesical chemotherapies, some feel that intravesical chemotherapy may have a better risk-benefit ratio than BCG. Indeed, the AUA statement at the time of BCG shortage in 2020 indicated that "intravesical chemotherapy should be used as the first-line option for patients with intermediate-risk NMIBC." Thus, the patient should undergo induction intravesical chemotherapy rather than foregoing therapy with observation. Nadofaragene firadenovec is approved for BCG unresponsive NMIBC and should be reserved for the salvage setting. Neither partial nor radical cystectomy would be appropriate in a treatment-naive patient with non-muscle invasive disease.

question: A 71-year-old man has an incidentally discovered left renal lesion shown in images. Physical examination, laboratory studies, and chest imaging are normal. The next step is: View Images
rationale: Bosniak 1 and 2 lesions have close to 0% risk of malignancy and do not require additional follow-up or imaging. Bosniak 2F lesions (multiple thin septa, minimal wall thickening, perceived enhancement, calcification) have up to 10% risk of malignancy and should be followed, while Bosniak 3 lesions have 50% risk of malignancy and Bosniak 4 lesions have up to 90% risk of malignancy. This patient has a Bosniak 2F lesion and should have repeat imaging in six months instead of no further follow-up, which is an option for Bosniak 1 and 2 cysts. Biopsy should not be performed as there is no nodular component to biopsy. Given the low chance of malignancy in this Bosniak 2F cyst, ablation and surgery are not indicated.

question: PARP inhibitors (poly-adenosine diphosphate [ADP]-ribose polymerase inhibitors) target tumors with defects in the pathway involving:
rationale: PARP inhibitors (poly-adenosine diphosphate [ADP]-ribose polymerase inhibitors) have shown activity in tumors with defects in DNA repair capabilities. Specifically, the PARP inhibitor olaparib is approved for the treatment of ovarian cancer with a BRCA1/2 mutation. PARP inhibitors have produced durable responses in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer associated with BRCA2 germline mutations and in the subset of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and somatic gene mutations in DNA repair genes (BRCA1/2, ATM, Fanconi's anemia genes and CHEK2) as detected by next generation sequencing. Drugs such as abiraterone and enzalutamide target the androgen pathway. The mTOR inhibitors, temsirolimus and everolimus, are approved for the treatment of metastatic kidney cancer. Microtubule inhibitors, including the taxanes (docetaxel), target the mitotic spindle. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors, such as sunitinib, pazopanib, and sorafenib, target tyrosine kinase receptor signaling and are all approved for treating metastatic renal cancer.

question: A 61-year-old man with Gleason 4+3=7 prostate cancer has a nadir PSA of 0.5 ng/mL after XRT and six months of leuprolide. Five years later, his PSA steadily increases to 2.8 ng/mL. PSMA PET scan is negative for metastatic disease. Prostate MRI T2 and apparent diffusion coefficient images are shown. The next step is:
rationale: This patient has biochemical recurrence after XRT, defined by the Phoenix Consensus definition as an increase in PSA of at least 2 ng/mL above nadir. Evaluation and management of biochemical recurrence after XRT should incorporate patient as well as clinical factors. This patient represents a candidate for salvage local therapy based on his age, original disease staging, and current PSA. Evaluation of such a patient should include re-staging imaging as well as an assessment for the presence of viable disease within the prostate (i.e., biopsy) in those whose imaging is negative for metastatic disease. Multiparametric MRI may be utilized to identify potentially concerning lesions within the prostate and thereby guide subsequent biopsy. Of note, following XRT, gland atrophy and fibrosis may result in a diffusely decreased T2 signal and thereby render this sequence less reliable for the detection of recurrent tumor. The images here demonstrate an area of slightly more focal T2 hypointensity in the posterior peripheral zone of the mid to lower gland that is associated with moderately restricted diffusion. Overall, the findings are suspicious for recurrent prostate cancer and should be used for a subsequent MRI-guided biopsy. In a patient who would be a candidate for local salvage therapy who has a work-up demonstrating a lesion within the prostate of concern for active cancer, biopsy is indicated. In this case, MRI-fusion targeted biopsy with or without concurrent systematic biopsy would be indicated because of the findings on MRI. Systematic biopsy alone would be insufficient. Meanwhile, apalutamide is a nonsteroidal anti-androgen that binds directly to the ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor (AR) and inhibits AR nuclear translocation, DNA binding, and transcription. The efficacy of apalutamide among patients with non-metastatic CRPC was demonstrated in the Phase 3 SPARTAN trial and has been FDA approved for use in this setting. However, the agent is not approved for use in patients with castration-sensitive biochemical recurrence as here. Thus, for such a patient without evidence of systemic disease who is a candidate for local therapy, further evaluation with prostate biopsy to establish the presence of disease in the prostate would facilitate offering local therapy, which would represent the patient's best long-term chance for cure. Nevertheless, prior to initiating salvage local therapy (prostatectomy, cryosurgery, brachytherapy, etc.), viable disease in the prostate should be documented with biopsy.

question: A 23-year-old man undergoes left orchiectomy for testicular cancer (90% seminoma, 10% teratoma and no lymphovascular invasion). Serum tumor markers and CXR are normal. CT scan is shown. The next step is:

options.A: repeat CT scan and tumor markers in eight weeks.

rationale: This patient has a para-aortic lymph node < 1 cm, which is equivocal for metastases. There is also a small retrocaval area which is the crus of the diaphragm. Risk factors for retroperitoneal metastases from stage 1 non-seminoma are predominant embryonal carcinoma and lymphovascular invasion. With neither of these present (as in this patient), the risk of metastases is approximately 15-20%, and surveillance is recommended in a compliant patient. According to the AUA Guidelines, in patients with normal serum tumor markers and equivocal imaging findings for metastasis, a solitary lymph node < 15 mm should be approached cautiously (particularly if outside the primary landing zone), and consideration should be given to repeat imaging in six to eight weeks. Adjuvant chemotherapy (BEP x 1 or 2) or RPLND are management options for clinical stage 1 non- seminoma with high-risk features or non-compliant patients. Retroperitoneal radiation is never given for non-seminoma but is used for some patients with pure seminoma. PET scans are never indicated for evaluation of patients with early-stage testicular cancer, primarily since teratoma is not PET-avid. Four cycles of BEP would never be given in this setting, as it is used for patients with IGCCCG intermediate or poor-risk categorization. If this patient ultimately required chemotherapy (i.e., elevated tumor markers in eight weeks), it would be a good-risk regimen (i.e., BEP x 3 or EP x 4).

question: A 50-year-old man has a large right renal mass with tumor thrombus extending into the atrium. Under hypothermia and circulatory arrest, he has a nephrectomy with removal of the tumor thrombus. The most frequent significant complication is:
rationale: Hypothermia and circulatory arrest is the treatment of choice for a renal tumor with this level of cephalad extension. This technique has several potential complications, such as central nervous system or hepatic damage, but the most common difficulty associated with this technique is hemorrhage associated with platelet and clotting factor dysfunction. Tumor emboli can occur but are relatively uncommon. Utilization of cardiopulmonary bypass limits the possibility of embolic events.

question: A 54-year-old man with normal erectile function and minimal LUTS completes neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a solitary muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder neck with associated CIS. Cystoscopy, DRE, laboratory, and staging evaluations are normal. He prioritizes maintenance of sexual function. The next step is:

options.A: cystoscopy and imaging in three months.
options.C: partial cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymph node dissection.
options.D: nerve-sparing radical cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymph node dissection.
options.E: prostate-sparing cystectomy with bilateral pelvic lymph node dissection.

rationale: The presence of CIS - which is often multifocal - renders partial cystectomy not the optimal treatment approach here. Likewise, the presence of CIS has been associated with adverse outcomes among patients treated with trimodal therapy, and thus, particularly in such a young patient, chemotherapy plus XRT would not represent the optimal management strategy. Further, residual disease has been found at cystectomy in up to 25-30% of patients who demonstrate a clinical response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC), and up to 50% of patients treated with NAC who do not undergo cystectomy experience disease recurrence in the bladder. Thus, current guidelines recommend radical cystectomy (rather than surveillance) following NAC for patients with muscle- invasive bladder cancer. While prostate or prostate capsule sparing may be considered to preserve sexual function, bladder neck, and prostatic urethral involvement are contraindications. Indeed, prostatic urethral involvement from bladder cancer and/or prostate adenocarcinoma has been found in up to 40% of patients at cystectomy. The presence of CIS, with its multifocality, additionally makes prostate-sparing not advisable. Instead, nerve-sparing (preservation of the neurovascular bundles) may be performed at cystectomy for patients without evidence of locally advanced disease in order to preserve sexual function.

question: A ten-year-old boy has self-limited scrotal pain. An ultrasound is shown. The next step is:

options.B: ultrasound and tumor markers in six months.
options.C: CT scan of chest and abdomen.

rationale: This child has diffuse testicular microlithiasis with a typical radiographic appearance. There is no need to consider any type of treatment in this child. The most important aspect of his care will be close observation and the need for self-exam. Testicular microlithiasis is present in more than 5% of healthy young men. Most studies now demonstrate that it does not appear to be a premalignant lesion although the importance of self-exam needs to be emphasized to these patients. Further evaluation with tumor markers or imaging is not indicated. Thus, similar to adults, the most important aspect of follow-up is the need for self-exam in older children and parental exam in younger children. There is no indication for surgical intervention, including biopsy or radical orchiectomy.

question: A 63-year-old obese man underwent partial penectomy for squamous cell carcinoma involving the corpus spongiosum. Pelvic CT scan demonstrates a 1.5 cm right inguinal lymph node that cannot be palpated. CT scans of the chest and abdomen are negative. The next step is:

options.A: antibiotics and repeat CT scan in six weeks.
options.B: CT-guided biopsy of the suspicious node.

rationale: This patient has pathologic stage T2 disease and is at high risk for occult inguinal node metastases. Therefore, this patient should undergo a bilateral inguinal lymph node dissection. CT-guided lymph node biopsy would not be required. Furthermore, while bilateral dynamic sentinel node biopsy has been utilized in this setting, unilateral dynamic sentinel node biopsy would not be sufficient. Antibiotics decrease the risk of inguinal wound infection, but the response of lymph nodes to antibiotic treatment should not influence the decision for surgical staging.

question: A 26-year-old man undergoes right radical orchiectomy for a NSGCT with lymphovascular invasion. CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and serum tumor markers done three weeks prior to orchiectomy were within normal limits. The next step is:

options.D: one cycle etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy.

rationale: This patient has high-risk (due to the presence of lymphovascular invasion) clinical stage 1 NSGCT (T2NOMO). While patients with clinical stage 1 NSGCT have the options for surveillance (with a 50% chance of recurrence, which will require three cycles of BEP chemotherapy), RPLND (with the possibility of needing adjuvant chemotherapy), and 1-2 cycles of BEP as adjuvant chemotherapy, the mainstay in managing patients with testicular cancer is accurate diagnosis and staging. As such, this patient needs repeat serum tumor markers before any therapeutic decisions are made. If tumor markers are still normal, he could proceed with surveillance, chemotherapy, or RPLND. One cycle of etoposide and cisplatin is not an option for clinical stage 1 NSGCT.

question: A 68-year-old woman underwent left radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy for a pT3b papillary RCC. The margin was microscopically positive at the IVC wall resection site. The next step is:

options.A: CT scan of the chest and abdomen in three months.

rationale: Per the AUA guidelines, this patient has Very High Risk disease (it is originally High Risk since it is a pT3, but it is upgraded to Very High Risk due to microscopic positive margin), and, therefore, needs a CT scan of the chest and abdomen in three months and should be managed as such with careful observation until visible disease is noted on imaging. PET-CT scan is not indicated in patients with RCC. Adjuvant pembrolizumab is an option for patients with pT3b RCC if they have clear cell, but not papillary, histology. XRT is not indicated for microscopically positive margins in patients with RCC who undergo surgery, either after partial nephrectomy, radical nephrectomy, or IVC thrombectomy. Re-resection of the IVC wall is not indicated unless the patient has a visible recurrence at the IVC wall on imaging that occurs in a delayed fashion (at least one to two years after surgery), and in the absence of distant metastatic disease.

question: The most common site of sympathetic nerve injury during a RPLND is the:

options.A: aortorenal ganglion adjacent to the renal hilum.
options.B: sympathetic chain inferior to the renal artery.
options.C: aortic plexus posterolateral to the aorta.
options.D: inferior mesenteric plexus adjacent to the inferior mesenteric artery.
options.E: hypogastric plexus anterior to the aortic bifurcation.

rationale: Nerve-sparing RPLND can be performed in the primary setting and in select patients in the post-chemotherapy setting. Normally, the post-ganglionic sympathetic fibers are identified below the renal vessels and are dissected out of the lymphatic tissue during a nerve-sparing RPLND. Regardless of the side of the dissection, great care is taken during dissection over the aortic bifurcation, as this is the site where the hypogastric plexus crosses anterior to the great vessels. This is where the sympathetic nerves are most vulnerable to injury, which is why the aortic bifurcation is not included in the modified RPLND template.
